idiom_name: Result<T, E> with Ok/Err, the ? operator and match
implementation_notes: Rust has no exceptions: Result<T, E> { Ok(T), Err(E) } is the standard contract, #[must_use] turns an ignored result into a compiler warning, and ? propagates a failure early (converting the error via From), so a sequence of fallible calls reads as straight-line code that returns Result. and_then/or_else/map/map_err/unwrap_or_else cover composition between calls, ok_or/ok_or_else lift Option into Result, and match or let-else consumes the value at the terminal handler. This is the pattern's native form; the design freedom is the error type - a library defines an enum implementing std::error::Error (derives help), while an application may prefer the type-erased anyhow form in the sibling variant.
pitfalls: unwrap()/expect() panic - the Rust form of the null dereference; keep them for tests and invariants and use ?/unwrap_or_else on production paths.
? converts the error via From, so a missing or careless From impl either fails to compile or collapses distinct errors into one variant; map_err when the mapping is deliberate.
An ignored Result is only a warning, not an error; libraries should keep unused_must_use denied in CI.

variants.name: anyhow::Result for applications
variants.implementation_notes: At application level the concrete error type often does not matter: anyhow supplies anyhow::Error, a trait-object error type, and the alias anyhow::Result<T>, written with ? exactly like std, plus context()/with_context() to attach human-readable frames and downcasting for the rare place that needs a concrete type (the README's cluster-info and detach examples are exactly this shape). Choose it in binaries and test helpers to avoid maintaining a large error enum; keep a concrete error type in libraries whose callers branch on variants, and convert at the crate boundary. The railway is unchanged - only the failure payload is type-erased.
pitfalls: anyhow::Error erases the type, so callers cannot exhaustively match variants; it must not appear in a library's public API where callers branch.
context() carries only a message string; machine-readable failure data has to survive as a typed error (custom enum or downcast), not as text.
